content: The University of Fribourg, located in the city of Fribourg, Switzerland, was officially established in 1889 by Georges Python, a local businessman. However, its origins can be traced back to 1580 with the founding of the Jesuit Seminary of St. Michel. The university offers courses in both French and German, and students are generally expected to understand both languages, except in certain departments like history and law, where curricula are available in both languages. The student population is approximately 10,000, with a notable number coming from the Italian-speaking region of Ticino. The Misericorde Campus, constructed between 1939 and 1942, was designed by architects Honegger and Dumas, who were students of the renowned Swiss architect Le Corbusier. This campus is considered architecturally significant. The university comprises five faculties: Catholic theology, law, natural sciences, arts, and economics & social sciences. Historically, the university's roots lie in the Jesuit College St. Michel, founded in 1580 by St. Pierre Canisius at the invitation of the Fribourg government. The establishment of Catholic higher education was a response to the rise of Protestant academies in Geneva, Lausanne, and Basel. In 1763, an Academy of Law was founded, housed in the Albertinum, which is now a Dominican residence. The cantonal library was established in 1834, incorporating works from Catholic monasteries. Following the expulsion of the Jesuits after the Sonderbund War, the College St. Michel was closed. Georges Python, who later became Director of Public Education, raised funds through a lottery and secured 2.5 million CHF from the canton to establish the university. Initially, lectures were held in the buildings of St. Michel, and the cantonal library was integrated with the university. The Academy of Law became the Faculty of Law, and the Dominicans managed the theological faculty under an agreement with the canton. By 1939, the university moved to a new campus on the former cemetery of Misericorde, and the St. Michel buildings were repurposed for a gymnasium, now known as College St. Michel. The Perolles campus was later constructed on the site of a former wagon factory. The city of Fribourg is 70% French-speaking and 30% German-speaking. This linguistic distribution, along with the historical dominance of French among the city’s aristocracy, explains the prevalence of French in university administration and the student union, AGEF (Association Générale des Étudiants Fribourgeois). In recent years, the university completed the construction of its Perolles 2 campus, which now houses the Faculty of Economics and Social Sciences. Plans are underway to build a Museum for Biblical Antiquities in the Tower of Henry IV after its renovation. Additionally, Fribourg has developed FriMat, a center of excellence in nanotechnology. As part of the BeNeFri association, which includes the universities of Bern, Neuchâtel, and Fribourg, students can take courses at any of the member universities and receive credit at their home institution. The university has adopted the Bologna process, awarding a BA after three years and an MA after an additional two years. The university does not have a centralized campus, with its buildings spread throughout the city. Key sites include Misericorde (humanities and central administration), Perolles (science), Perolles 2 (economics), Regina Mundi (psychology), BCU centrale (main library), Pierre Aeby (classical philology), Bonnesfontaines (pedagogy), and Stade St. Leonard (university stadium). The university observes several traditions. On Dies Academicus, held annually in November, no lectures are conducted. The day begins with Mass in the Chapel of the Collège St. Michel, followed by a solemn procession to the Aula Magna (Great Hall), where the rector and a guest speaker deliver addresses, and honorary degrees are awarded. Student guilds, dressed ceremonially with swords, participate in the event. These guilds, similar to student nations in Uppsala, Lund, and Helsinki, dine together weekly in uniform and were historically involved in dueling. Membership in these guilds is often advantageous for careers in business, politics, or law. The university also hosts a Day of Welcomes (Jour d'Accueil), akin to Freshers' Week, where new students are welcomed by the rector and the city’s mayor, followed by a meal at the university Mensa. Student life at the university includes sports such as skiing, fencing, ice hockey, football, and basketball. Unlike many universities, Fribourg does not have its own halls of residence. A minority of students live in foyers, often run by religious organizations, while most rent their own accommodations. Notable foyers include Cité St. Justin and the Salesianum. There is also a student housing cooperative known as REST. The university used to offer primary degrees lasting five to five and a half years, culminating in a Lizentiat (equivalent to a Master’s degree). With the Bologna reforms, students now receive a BA after three years and an MA after two additional years. Students are issued a tabella, a booklet in which they record attended lectures, signed by professors. Fribourg also has an active nightlife, with popular bars like Café Populaire and clubs such as To See and FMRA. The university’s seal features a cross and bishop’s ring, symbolizing its Catholic ethos, on a black and white shield representing the canton of Fribourg. This is being replaced by a blue logo with triangles representing the Alps and the university’s name in Latin. Notable alumni and faculty include Maurice Zermatten (writer and Schiller International Prize winner), Tariq Ramadan (philosopher and Islamic scholar), Michel Plancherel (mathematician), Alfred Gockel (physicist involved in the discovery of cosmic radiation), Gonzague de Reynold (writer and academic), Cardinal Gilberto Agustoni, and Cardinal Gaspard Mermillod. Benito Mussolini once worked as a stonemason on the university’s central library. The university holds the third-largest collection of Biblical antiquities in the world, after the British Museum and the Cairo Museum. During World War II, it collaborated with the University of Zurich to educate Polish prisoners of war. The Catholic Church annually collects funds during Masses across Switzerland, known as Fribourg Sunday, to provide scholarships for foreign priests through the Theology Faculty. To commemorate its centenary, La Poste issued a stamp featuring the figures Science and Sagesse.
